entries.title: Mitch McConnell Is Denying Republicans His Massive Cash Stash
entries.summary: The outgoing senator has nearly $7.4 million to part with before leaving office in January. So far, he’s sitting on it.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell is hoarding his committee’s wealth during a crucial midterms cycle for the Republican Party, according to a new federal filing.

When the Kentucky senator returned to Capitol Hill in September after a three-month, health-related absence, his campaign committee had nearly $7.4 million waiting for him.

But McConnell, who no longer has use for the money since he opted not to run for an eighth term, opted not to spread his wealth to any Republican Party committee or candidate campaign. That includes the Senate Leadership Fund and Texas PAC, political committees associated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who succeeded McConnell as the Republicans’ Senate leader.

Before McConnell leaves the Senate in January, his campaign committee has a few options for its surplus money.

Most urgently, McConnell’s committee can still donate up to $2,000 a piece to other Republican candidate committees. It may also transfer unlimited amounts to national party committees, such as the Republican National Committee or National Republican Senatorial Committee.

McConnell’s committee could also donate its millions to charities or nonprofit universities.

One organization McConnell is already connected to is the nonpartisan McConnell Center at the University of Louisville. The center was established in 1991 to encourage Kentucky’s top students to pursue higher education in their home state, and McConnell raised the initial funds for scholarships.

Other legal options include refunding donors or disgorging money to the U.S. Treasury’s general fund.
entries.author: Nicole Belcastro

entries.title: Graham Platner’s Campaign Paid a $20,000 Severance to His Wife
entries.summary: The campaign also forked over payments to other staffers after the Democrat dropped out of the Senate race in Maine.
entries.content:
Graham Platner announced July 8 he was dropping out of the race for Senate in Maine.

Nine days later, his campaign paid his wife, Amy Gertner, $20,246 for “severance payroll.”

That’s part of the more than $350,000 Platner’s campaign paid out in severances, according to a filing with the Federal Election Commission. Others on the payroll received between $3,500 and $20,000 each in severance. Gertner received the most.

Gertner had a visible role on Platner’s campaign. When he came under scrutiny for sending sexually explicit texts to other women, Gertner filmed a selfie-style video defending her marriage and calling the stories “gossip.” Platner has denied the allegations, which later included a former girlfriend saying he had sexually assaulted her.

Campaign staffers, including Gertner, also received a $979 “win bonus” on July 3, a month after Platner’s primary victory.

Several staffers received severance payments of about $9,000. Some of them, per their personal LinkedIn pages, are current college students.

The campaign also paid out more than $70,000 in refunds to donors.

Platner’s team had more than $1.7 million on hand at the beginning of July. After campaign expenditures, severance and refunds, the campaign ended September with just about $99,000 remaining.

None of the leftover money went to Troy Jackson, Platner’s replacement in the race against incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins — perhaps due to political optics.

“That’s ‘Nazi accused rapist’ money,” a Democratic strategist told The Washington Sun in July. “The best thing he could do is give it to a women’s charity, specifically an organization supporting rape victims.”

Platner’s treasurer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sara Gideon, the Democrat who challenged Collins in 2020, still has $2 million in her campaign accounts. In recent months, she distributed $310,000 to Maine Democrats and $70,000 to other Democratic candidates across the country.
entries.author: Chase Pellegrini de Paur

entries.title: Who’s Running Roger Marshall’s Campaign? His Campaign Filings Don't Say.
entries.summary: The Republican, who is in a heated race in Kansas, is facing questions about whether his Senate office is fueling his reelection campaign.
entries.content:
Sen. Roger Marshall’s latest campaign finance filing is largely missing spending entries typical of nearly all campaign reports: Those described as wages, salaries or payroll.

The Kansas Republican, who is up for reelection in a competitive race as Democrats try to expand their Senate map, is facing scrutiny about whether he’s used taxpayer dollars to fund his reelection bid, including by using his official Senate staff as an extension of his campaign.

Marshall’s latest filing with the Federal Election Commission, covering campaign spending from mid-July through the end of September, does not appear to include any payments to full-time campaign staff.

A joint investigation published last week by MS NOW and Kansas Reflector reported that the Marshall campaign hadn’t cut a paycheck to campaign staff in the last five years, an arrangement that experts quoted in the piece called “extremely uncommon” for a Senate campaign. The article also listed a number of instances in which Marshall may have violated ethics rules by using his office’s funds for campaign purposes.

Marshall’s office and the Marshall campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Marshall’s chief of staff told MS NOW and Kansas Reflector that the campaign now has campaign staff, without providing evidence.

Congressional staffers are allowed to work for campaigns, but only under strict guidelines. The work must be done on staffers’ own time, outside of congressional offices and without congressional resources.

The FEC filing says Marshall’s campaign spent $5.3 million in the third quarter, raising about $801,000 and finishing with $922,000 cash on hand.

The FEC records also indicate the campaign spent a little more than $10,000 on outside consultants from July through September.

Marshall, who polling has found to be deadlocked with Democrat Adam Hamilton, is in need of additional support for his campaign operation. According to Axios, Chris Grant, a top Trump political adviser who has previously worked for Marshall, is part of the cavalry that’s been sent in to help Marshall’s campaign in the final stretch.

The Washington Sun previously reported that Republican PACs have moved millions of dollars of ads into Kansas to rescue Marshall’s reelection bid as some GOP operatives say the senator lacks a good ground game.
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: Labor's Trump-Appointed Watchdog Gets His Own Ethics Audit
entries.summary: Former Republican Rep. Anthony D’Esposito could face criminal charges if he is found to have violated objectivity standards.
entries.content:
Federal ethics investigators will audit the political conduct of Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, a former Long Island congressman accused of allowing partisan loyalties to affect his responsibilities as an impartial internal watchdog.

The U.S. Office of Special Counsel has “accepted the matter for review,” Newsday first reported Thursday, citing a letter sent this week to the nonprofit watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington. CREW filed the initial complaint against D’Esposito in April.

D’Esposito bristled when asked about the investigation, calling CREW a group of “political hacks” hawking “bogus nonsense.”

“It’s bullshit,” he told The Washington Sun Thursday evening. “I’ll keep exposing fraud and fighting for American workers.”

The ethics complaint against D’Esposito, who was appointed to the position last year by President Donald Trump, stems from a series of politically slanted social media posts the inspector general published using his official Labor Department X account.

He purportedly used the account to praise the president’s immigration and economic policies and congratulate him for his war efforts in Iran. In the April complaint, CREW chief executive Donald Sherman also pointed to numerous instances when D’Esposito accepted explicit direction from Trump and other administration officials.

“During his tenure as inspector general, D’Esposito has blurred the lines between official and political activities,” Sherman wrote.

The DOL inspector general is responsible for investigating fraud, waste and misconduct within the department and is legally required to remain objective and isolated from political pressures.

If the Office of Special Counsel finds that D’Esposito has flaunted objectivity standards, he could be fined, removed from office or face criminal prosecution for violating the Hatch Act's prohibitions against partisan activity.

Sherman also implored the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency to act. D’Esposito said in a statement to Newsday that the council — another group that oversees integrity complaints against cross-agency inspectors general — is “taking no further action.”

Representatives from the council and the OSC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Musk Settles Lawsuits Over His $1 Million Election Giveaways
entries.summary: The Tesla founder promised voters checks before the 2024 presidential election, which critics said constituted election bribery.
entries.content:
Elon Musk and his political action committee have agreed to settle two lawsuits that accused them of misleading voters with promises of $1 million checks before the 2024 presidential election and in a 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election.

Legal counsel for the parties notified a federal judge in Texas that they’d struck an agreement to end the dual class-action suits Thursday. Terms of the settlements are not public and still require court approval.

The plaintiffs in the two cases — Arizona residents Jacqueline McAferty and Joy Harvick — accused Musk and America PAC of coaxing ⁠voters in seven swing states into signing his 2024 petition to support free speech and gun rights and submitting personal information for what they were told was a chance to receive $1 million. The giveaway was part of Musk’s broader effort to return Donald Trump to the White House.

The cases’ central claim, according to court filings, is that America PAC representatives vetted potential recipients of the prize rather than simply drawing names from a hat.

Following that blueprint, the tech mogul took the tactic to the March 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election to urge voters to turn out for Brad Schimel, the state's former Republican attorney general.

“I will also personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote,” Musk said in a now-deleted post on X.

Musk has already escaped a potential legal battle concerning his promises in Wisconsin: La Crosse County District Attorney Tim Gruenke declined to charge the tech mogul with election bribery in August, despite the state elections commission’s earlier ruling that he had likely broken the law. Gruenke, a Democrat, said no jury would have found Musk’s actions constituted election bribery.

America PAC, which is primarily funded by Musk himself, spent millions to support Schimel, who later lost to Susan Crawford.


The Tesla founder has denied the allegations of engaging in election bribery.

The Arizona settlements come weeks before November’s consequential elections. Musk, the wealthiest person in the world, has personally contributed over $275 million — more than any other person — to support the Republican Party’s efforts to retain its congressional majorities.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Mary Peltola Dismisses Reports of Angry Outbursts as ‘Gossip’ During Debate
entries.summary: For the first time, the Democrat running in the high-stakes Alaska Senate race publicly addressed the reporting by The New York Times.
entries.content:
Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska’s Senate race, directly addressed allegations of mistreatment of former staffers for the first time on Thursday, calling them “outright fabrications” and “mass exaggerations of the truth” in a debate.

Peltola, who is running against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a close and widely watched race, has dodged questions on the campaign trail about the report by The New York Times from late September detailing mistreatment of staff. But at the hour-long Senate debate, the first time the candidates had faced off in such a setting, it came up several times.

Sullivan seemed eager to make it an issue, and brought up the allegations during an unrelated debate question.

“Take a look at how she treats Alaskans when the cameras are off. Look at that New York Times story,” he said, arguing it revealed a “character flaw.”

He alluded to some of the outlet’s reporting beyond Peltola’s behavior toward staff, including her alleged use of slurs.

The two began talking over each other, with Sullivan adding, “It’s The New York Times, read the article.”

Peltola jumped in to say the allegations were “gossip.”

The moderator threatened to shut off their microphones if necessary.

Later, a moderator asked Peltola directly about the allegations.

“I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day,” she said. “I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth.”

“I really am very concerned about making sure that we are respectful and respectful of all people, and again, this campaign is not about me on my worst day,” she added.

The Democratic candidate also suggested that the allegations likely emerged because her campaign is a threat to Sullivan. The incumbent senator once again circled back to the subject, pointing out that the report was not published by “conservative media” but rather the Times.

The Times reported that former staffers said Peltola had a history of frustration with staff throughout her campaign and as a member of the House of Representatives. It outlined an instance of her allegedly shoving a staffer, which her campaign characterized to the outlet as a bump. The report also included her alleged use of slurs, which Sullivan referenced as he attacked her over the article.

The story also described a text in which Peltola said of someone, “I hope she dies of a botched abortion.” That was also used as an attack line by Sullivan.

In a statement to the Times, her campaign spokesperson denied that she had a pattern of abusive behavior and cited a period of grief following the deaths of Peltola’s mother and husband in 2023.

The allegations shook the race in the closing stretch of the campaign, prompting an intraparty feud among Democrats about whether the staffers who shared their accounts with the Times had been too sensitive.

It was not a debate many Democrats liked taking up oxygen, given that the Alaska race has emerged as one of the most competitive in the country, with The Cook Political Report rating it a “toss-up.” Sullivan has served in his seat for two terms and Peltola was previously a U.S. House representative for Alaska’s at-large district.

It was clear how high the stakes were for both of them, as those were not the only heated exchanges.

Peltola appeared to read off notecards for much of the debate, which Sullivan noticed in real time.

"We weren't supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?" he asked. (The moderators said no.) "I'm just watching my opponent read."

“I’m prepared,” Peltola responded.
entries.author: Ellie Fivas

entries.title: Donald Trump’s Legal Fund Is Flirting With Insolvency
entries.summary: Save America PAC is $1.9 million in debt after heavy summer spending.
entries.content:
Save America PAC — President Donald Trump’s preferred vehicle for paying legal bills — spent more than $5.1 million on legal bills during the third quarter, or around $56,000 per day, according to the committees’ latest filing to the Federal Election Commission.

That kind of spending has sent the leadership PAC — which is often pushing money out the door faster than it can come in — into legal debt topping $1.9 million.

Never Surrender, another Trump leadership PAC, helped to bail out Save America PAC by transferring from its account almost all of the $4.8 million Save America took in during the third quarter.

But it wasn’t enough to cover all of Save America’s legal bills, or the other $343,000 Save America spent on media consulting, payroll and other expenses, FEC records indicate.

Trump is a convicted felon who has faced numerous criminal and civil proceedings during the past several years, including a 2023 trial during which a New York jury found him liable for sexual abuse. Trump has also gone on the legal offensive of late, personally suing media organizations.

Neither Save America nor the White House immediately responded to requests for comment.

Save America has collectively paid more than two-dozen firms about $20.4 million for legal services and consulting since January 2025, when Trump began his second presidential term, according to FEC records. The PAC owes money to 12 of those firms, including two based in London.

Save America owes $761,000 to Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, the legal giant that has represented Trump in several high-profile legal battles, including the president’s unsuccessful appeal to the Supreme Court to overturn the $83 million defamation verdict that the writer E. Jean Carroll won.

The PAC also owes $663,000 to NechelesLaw LLP. Susan Necheles was one of the defense attorneys who cross-examined the adult-film actress Stormy Daniels during Trump’s “hush money” trial in 2024.

Brito PLLC, a Florida-based firm that has represented the president’s cases against news media giants including ABC News and The New York Times, is also owed $239,000.

Save America is also in debt $34,000 to the Dhillon Law Group, the firm founded by Harmeet Dhillon, who now serves in the Trump administration as assistant attorney general for the civil rights division at the Department of Justice.

The PAC also owes thousands of dollars to firms including New York-based criminal defense firm Tacopina, Seigel & DeOreo; Houston-based patent litigation firm Taylor Dykema PLLC; and civil rights and criminal defense firm James Otis Law Group LLC, among others.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno

entries.title: Kari Lake’s Old Senate Committee Is Still Stiffing Campaign Creditors
entries.summary: Lake awaits confirmation as U.S. ambassador to Jamaica. Her former campaign vendors together await more than $1 million.
entries.content:
Republican Kari Lake’s 2024 Senate campaign loss to Democrat Ruben Gallego is long behind her — except for the over $1 million in debt her campaign still owes two years later, according to a new Federal Election Commission filing.

Lake’s old campaign committee owes more than $328,000 to Opn Sesame for texting and telemarketing services and almost $278,000 to TAG LLC for “digital consulting & fundraising service.” The remaining over $400,000 in debts for online advertising and fundraising, however, are marked as “disputed.”

The seven-figure debt lingers as President Donald Trump’s nomination of Lake as U.S. ambassador to Jamaica has stalled — she has not yet received Senate confirmation despite the president nominating her in May.

The Lake committee isn’t without cash; it has nearly half a million on hand as of Sept. 30, according to its latest financial statement.

It’s also still processing a stream of contributions. Since July, Lake’s committee marked about $1,500 worth of this income as “debt retirement," meaning the money would directly go to paying off the campaign’s debt.

In the last year, the Lake campaign’s total debt fell by around $6,000, according to FEC filings, or about 0.6% of its current debt. Lake did not immediately respond to The Sun’s request for comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a Washington Sun inquiry.

Lake, an Arizona news broadcaster before her foray into politics marked by loyalty to Trump, has remained in the president’s close political orbit.

Last year, Trump appointed Lake as the “acting CEO” of the U.S. Agency for Global Media, which oversees Voice of America among other state-run foreign media outfits. In her first year, she oversaw massive downsizing.

In March, a federal judge ruled that both her chief role and cuts were illegal. Trump’s nomination of Lake for ambassador followed soon after.
entries.author: Kyle Chouinard

entries.title: MS Forced Him to Retire From Politics. He Found a New Voice by Painting.
entries.summary: John Czwartacki spent decades as a political communicator, but he said painting felt like he “learned every language in the world.”
entries.content:
For decades, John Czwartacki made a career out of words.

He had worked and lived in D.C. since the ’90s, but in 2020, multiple sclerosis forced him into early retirement. The chronic disease, which affects the central nervous system, has been part of his life since his diagnosis in 1993. As it progressed, it affected his voice, making it increasingly difficult for him to communicate the way he once had.

“By 2020, I got to do so many things, so many great things. I traveled. I got jobs,” Czwartacki, better known as CZ, told The Washington Sun. “Unfortunately, I had the real reality of like, okay, well, I can't work in government. I can't work in a social office. Doctors are not really happy with me doing that.”

A longtime Republican communicator, Czwartacki served as press secretary for then-Rep. John Boehner and later as communications director for the Office of Management and Budget during President Donald Trump’s first term. His job was to shape messages, write speeches and explain the work of government.

For years following his retirement, Czwartacki struggled with what he described as a pent-up feeling, searching for a way to express an experience that spoken words could no longer fully capture.

Then, in November 2025, he bought a paintbrush and starter paints.

“Why is that? I'm not entirely sure,” he said. “I created pieces of art that I didn't expect to create, right? I didn't see that going in.”

As multiple sclerosis changed his relationship with his body and senses, painting opened up a new way to experience and interpret the world.

“I feel like a whole new set of senses was opened up to me. So it's like, wow!” he said. “A whole new suite of tactics to articulate myself are now available.”

For someone who had spent his career communicating through language, the discovery was revelatory.

“They're not things like words but you feel them and what is going on here is so cool as someone who has loved to communicate his whole life,” he said. “I'm like it's a whole new way to do it and I'm like, this is astounding to me.”
Mick Mulvaney, John Czwartacki (5171x3447, AR: 1.50)Czwartacki began experimenting with vibrant colors, fascinated by how they interacted on the canvas.

“Putting them close to each other and they would sing to each other and talk and leave you with a feeling of anticipation,” he said.

Less than a year after picking up a paintbrush, Czwartacki held his first art show on Oct. 8. The displayed paintings offered glimpses into the physical and emotional realities of living with a disease that has altered how he moves through the world — and how he sees himself.

The show was held in partnership with Survivors for Solutions, the nonprofit Czwartacki founded in 2022 to advocate for people facing health challenges who often struggle to make their voices heard in Washington.

Czwartacki painted “Hold On” while experiencing vertigo. Against a black background, white paint smears across the canvas, while a bright orange circle sits in the upper right corner.

The result is disorienting, an attempt to translate a physical sensation into something viewers can experience for themselves.

Another painting is an abstract self-portrait, a piece Czwartacki initially dreaded making.

He worried about his ability to draw recognizable features — “a nose or an ear or an eye” — but his son asked him to try.

The skeletal outline is fractured, he said, while the green near the bottom represents grounding. The background uses the same orange found in “Hold On,” a color that stands out against the more subdued elements of the portrait.

“I saw myself as incomplete and broken — still telling the story with things like this and also the MS,” he said. “And then the orange is kind of like shouting at you — it's paradoxical.”

The work does not attempt to neatly resolve the contradictions of his experience. Instead, the paintings hold them together: brokenness and expression, frustration and discovery, the limitations imposed by illness and the possibilities that remain.
John Czwartacki's paintings (5437x3624, AR: 1.50)Tina Robinson has known Czwartacki for over five years and founded an MS support group with him. She said he and his art are “proof that MS doesn’t get the final word.”

“As a patient myself, it’s inspiring to see him use the gift of time that new treatments have given us to find a new voice through his art,” Robinson said. “I hope his story inspires others living with chronic illness like MS or any challenging disease to take on new challenges and hold on to hope.”

Czwartacki may no longer be shaping political messages from inside the government, but he has not abandoned the impulse that drove him to the profession in the first place. He is still telling stories. He is still trying to make people feel something. He has simply found a different medium.

“I felt very proud of myself for my skill with English and my ability to write things and speeches and op-eds,” he said. “But when I learned to paint like this, I felt like I was taught every language in the world.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Trump’s Endorsement May Not Matter in the Next House Republican Leadership Race
entries.content:
There’s a big factor missing from the next race to lead House Republicans: President Donald Trump.

With House Republicans facing the prospect that they could be in the minority next year, and Trump himself entering the back end of his own lame-duck period, some believe the president’s influence won’t close the deal for Mike Johnson if he runs to remain the top elected leader.

“Not one bit,” one GOP lawmaker, given anonymity to speak freely, told The Washington Sun when asked if Trump’s endorsement matters. “Especially if we have lost, because people will blame him.”

Trump’s unique power has loomed over leadership races since Kevin McCarthy's bruising bid in 2023, when the president’s endorsement and personal phone calls helped sway some holdouts from blocking McCarthy’s path.

Trump intervened again during the next speaker’s race, after McCarthy was ousted 10 months later, when he thwarted Rep. Tom Emmer’s chances with a simple Truth Social post calling the Republican whip “totally out of touch.” And when Mike Johnson sought a full term as speaker in 2024, the president pressured some reluctant members to coalesce around Johnson to help him secure the gavel in 2025.

Heading into the next Congress, Republican lawmakers are split on Trump’s pull, with some saying it’s “not nearly as much” this round and others saying the president’s opinion would have some impact.

Johnson has made it clear he wants to lead his conference, whether or not Republicans maintain the majority. He currently has the backing of the president, who still thinks fondly of the Louisianan, according to two White House officials. But the path for Johnson won’t be easy, members say.

“He will not run unopposed,” one senior GOP member said.

Asked to comment on the speaker’s plan, a Johnson spokesperson referred The Sun to recent interviews with Johnson saying he believes Republicans will keep the majority and that he will remain the top leader.

But in an interview with Fox News recently, Johnson said he was unsure of what his next chapter would be if Democrats flip control of the House, saying that “if God moves on our hearts” he could go back to his hometown of Shreveport to start a “lawn business.”

Days later, in an interview with CBS News, he clarified his comments were "tongue in cheek” and added, “I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in a divided government” if House Republicans lost the majority.

There are two other potential candidates laying the groundwork to lead the GOP conference next year. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise is popular with many members, who view him as personable, loyal and a savvy operator. And then there’s House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, who has been traveling and raising money for colleagues over the past year in what many view as building support to run for the top post.

Even if Johnson had Trump’s backing, that hasn’t always helped in the past. In 2023, following McCarthy’s ouster, Trump publicly backed Jordan for speaker over Scalise. However, on the private ballot, Scalise came out victorious.

Similarly, when Jordan did eventually get the nomination after Scalise dropped out, Trump’s endorsement didn’t translate into votes on the floor, as a bloc of members opposed him on multiple ballots.

Following the defeat, Jordan has been attempting to rebuild his image into someone who is a team player. He’s been in constant contact with the Republican conference through weekly, and at times daily, check-ins with his colleagues across the conference, multiple members told The Sun.

“Jim Jordan calls me every week, and he knows I wasn’t for him last time and not for him this time, and yet he still calls,” one lawmaker told The Sun.

Trump will have a bit more sway if Republicans retain the majority because lawmakers will have to publicly cast their ballot for speaker on the House floor. But, in the minority, members will vote via secret ballot the week after the midterms in a closed-door election, where Republican lawmakers say Trump’s power diminishes dramatically.

White House spokesperson Liz Huston, asked about Trump’s role, told The Sun, “President Trump is focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

“If we win, then POTUS runs the show, as always,” one lawmaker, given anonymity to speak candidly, told The Sun. “But if we lose, he’s got a lot less stroke.”
entries.author: Kadia Goba, Reese Gorman
